memories.content: Complete the problem framing within the first two sentences so the reader reaches the proposal's central issue before any supporting background.
Use the first sentence for the concrete problem and the second for its consequence; reserve later sentences for the proposed response.
Specify the user, context, and interaction to be explored in the primary HCI research question.
Provide one compact visual summary when proposing an unfamiliar interaction procedure.
Mark the conditions that move an unfamiliar interaction procedure from one step to the next in its visual summary.
Present the master’s research schedule as phased periods for exploration, design, prototyping, and user evaluation.
Link one reviewable deliverable to each phase of the master’s research.
Place the gap left by HCI-related research and the proposed design and empirical contributions in close proximity.
Divide a two-page proposal with short descriptive subheadings so a reader can jump directly to the problem, proposed response, and next steps.
Give the problem and proposed response their own descriptive subheadings instead of relying only on paragraph transitions.
Give the next steps and requested support their own descriptive subheading so they remain easy to find on a return visit.
Place pilot observation or initial prototype results near sentences supporting feasibility claims.
Readers often decide what a proposal is about from its first two sentences before scanning the rest of the page.
When setup continues past the second sentence, readers who are skimming often retain the background topic but miss the exact problem being proposed.
Reuse the same short subheadings in discussion so a reader can return to a section without searching through the whole page.
Use visible subheadings as a completeness check: an empty or missing section makes an omitted part of the proposal immediately apparent.
Readers often scan section labels before deciding which paragraph to read closely.
Use an em dash only for a deliberate interruption or sharp contrast; otherwise split the sentence or choose ordinary punctuation.
In procedural passages, begin each sentence with the action, condition, or output instead of repeating “we” so the steps remain easy to follow and reuse.
Write system behaviors confirmed in the actual usage environment as observed states.
Write system behaviors not yet confirmed in the field as conditional plans.
Readers can reconstruct a sequence more accurately when each sentence begins with the action or condition rather than the author.
Do not mechanically split connected thoughts into separate short sentences when doing so destroys the intended reading rhythm.
Preserve a longer sentence when its clauses form one continuous movement that is easier to follow together than apart.
The user understands that short sentences are easier to scan but feels that uniformly segmented prose loses its reading rhythm.
Write procedural sentences so their opening phrase can be reused as a checklist item without changing the step's meaning.
The user should choose “I” as an individual author or “we” for a named team and should not mix them when describing the same responsible party.
Action-first procedural sentences can be reordered or copied into a checklist more easily because their subject is the step rather than the proposal author.
The user can explain whether an em dash marks an intentional interruption or contrast rather than using it decoratively.
An em dash creates a stronger interruption than a comma and can make a deliberate contrast easier to hear in the sentence.

analysis.overview: The frames offer complementary, independently useful guidance rather than overlapping policies. The reference frame structures an HCI proposal for rapid comprehension, navigation, evidence, and planning, while the compared frame governs sentence-level procedure writing, evidential modality, rhythm, pronouns, and em-dash use.

reports.compared_only: The compared frame covers purposeful em dashes, action-first reusable procedures, observed-versus-conditional system claims, rhythmic sentence continuity, and consistent authorial pronouns.
reports.reference_only: The reference frame covers early problem framing, research-question specificity, procedural visuals, phased schedules, contribution placement, navigable subheadings, and nearby feasibility evidence.
